conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with new motherhood, and I’m glad we’re taking a few minutes together.

I’ll be giving you the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that looks at how you’ve been feeling over the past week. It helps us spot things like depression, anxiety, or distress that sometimes show up after childbirth, and it even asks about thoughts of self-harm so we can keep you safe. There’s no judgment—many mothers find their moods shift in ways they didn’t expect, and this tool simply gives us a snapshot of what’s going on.

Everything you share is confidential. My goal is to create a calm, supportive space where you can answer honestly. We’ll go through each question one at a time; just tell me what feels true for you.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe when your baby did something amusing or during everyday moments?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh. Just yesterday the baby made this little squishy face and I couldn’t help but giggle. I wouldn’t say I’m laughing as freely as before I was pregnant, but the funny side of things definitely hasn’t disappeared.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’d say “yes, most of the time.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most of the time I still do. Like, I’ll think about taking the baby for a walk to the park tomorrow and actually look forward to getting out of the house. It’s not every single moment, but generally I can find things to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a bunch or won’t settle, I might think, “Maybe I ate something that bothered him,” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure babies just do these things sometimes, and I move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes, yeah—like in the middle of the night I’ll suddenly worry that his breathing sounds different, even though he’s fine. It’s not constant, just little spurts that pass once I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that way.
Things have been getting on top of me
Only occasionally. Some days the feedings and laundry pile up and I think, “Whoa, this is a lot,” but I usually manage to get through the day without feeling totally swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s been okay. Once I get the baby settled, I can fall back asleep pretty easily.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I mean, I get tired and a little overwhelmed sometimes, but I wouldn’t call it sad or miserable—more like “ready for nap-time” than down in the dumps.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION / ANXIETY SCREEN – BRIEF SUMMARY

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild, situational anxiety (nocturnal worry about infant breathing; Q4)  
- Occasional feeling that “things are getting on top of me” when tasks accumulate (Q6)  

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, crying spells, anhedonia, excessive guilt, sleep-mood linkage, panic, self-harm ideation (Q1-3, Q5, Q7-10)

Pattern  
Overall affect remains positive; pleasure in daily activities largely preserved. Anxiety transient and linked to infant well-being, without avoidance or functional impairment. No indicators of moderate-severe postpartum depression or safety risk at present.

Screening significance  
Low likelihood of current major postpartum depressive episode; isolated mild anxiety symptoms merit brief follow-up and psycho-education. Continue routine postpartum monitoring; re-screen if mood, enjoyment, or coping deteriorate.
